title: Massachusetts Voters Will Decide Whether Towns Must Allow Smaller Homes
summary:
Massachusetts is one of the most expensive states in the country for housing. Now voters there will decide on a ballot measure that aims to make it easier to build smaller, cheaper homes.

Many cities and towns across the U.S. have rules called minimum lot sizes. These rules say a single-family house must sit on a piece of land of a certain size. In Massachusetts, most such rules require at least an acre, which is about 40,000 square feet. That is nearly the size of a football field without the end zones.

The ballot measure would require towns to allow homes on lots as small as 5,000 square feet, about the size of a basketball court. It would not apply to Boston, which has its own rules. If it passes, Massachusetts would join a growing number of states that have made similar changes.

Supporters say big lot rules mean fewer homes get built, and the ones that are built tend to be large and expensive. Housing economist Andrew Mikula, who is leading the push, said many older homes on small lots would be illegal to build today. Supporters also say high prices are pushing young workers out of the state. Polling suggests broad support for the measure.

Jamie Sharken, a 34-year-old renter, told NPR she shares a house with three other people and doubts she can afford to buy a home. She supports the idea.

Critics do not like the state taking control away from local towns. They also question whether the homes will really be affordable. A Lexington official showed NPR an old house on a small lot that had been expanded and was listed for nearly $1.3 million.
why_it_matters: Rules about land size shape how many homes get built and who can afford to live in a community, an issue many states are now facing.

background_read: Zoning rules are local laws that decide what can be built on each piece of land in a city or town, such as houses, stores or apartments.
Minimum lot size rules set how much land a single-family house needs, so larger requirements mean fewer, bigger homes fit in an area.
When there are not enough homes for everyone who wants one, prices and rents tend to rise.
In some states, voters can decide a rule directly through a ballot measure instead of waiting for lawmakers to pass it.
